name: Erik Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that doesn't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on my father-in-law's farm, Walter's place up on the ridge road. We run about forty beef cattle and twenty acres of potatoes, and some barley for the cattle. I was a builder's labourer for twenty years, then Walter's back went five years ago and Ruth asked if I'd step in. So I'm forty-three and still being told how to stack bales by a man of seventy-four.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does a normal day go?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Up at six, feed and water the cattle, check the fences, then whatever Walter says over his tea. In the season it's planting, then hoeing, then lifting the potatoes and grading them by hand in the barn, which is slow but we do it right. Walter pays me what the farm can spare, which isn't much, and Ruth works mornings at the church office. We've got Daniel and Grace, a mortgage on our house in the village, and not even a month saved. I don't use computers if I can help it, Ruth does the forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. A lot of clever people in cities got excited about a talking computer, and the cows still needed feeding. I'd say it after church to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Means things go on as they are, and that suits me. I didn't come to farming for excitement, I came because Walter's back gave out and family is family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going exactly as I am. Learn the potatoes properly, maybe get Walter to show me the sprayer at last. Nothing else, I'd not touch any of that AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Walter think of all the AI talk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He says the same about it as he said about the internet: it'll sell you something you don't need. He's mostly right. He still keeps the herd book in a ledger from the feed merchant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is money a worry, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's always a worry. Potatoes went for nothing last year because the big packers set the price. But I'd rather work harder than take a handout, that's how I was raised.

S0.say: He'd say clever city people got excited about a talking computer while the cows still needed feeding. He'd say this after church to anyone who'd listen.
S0.think: Privately a plateau suits him, since he came to farming out of family duty, not for excitement. Things carrying on as they are is what he wants.
S0.do: Keeps working exactly as before on his father-in-law's farm. Learns the potatoes properly and asks to be shown the sprayer, without touching AI tools.
S0.quote: I didn't come to farming for excitement, I came because Walter's back gave out and family is family.
S0.fieldNote: Family duty is the core of his story: he farms because his father-in-law needed him. Money worries are blamed on big packers, but he'd rather work harder than take help. His resistance to technology is shared with the older generation he works for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the big companies doing what big companies do, and small farms like ours will have to dig in. Same as always. I'd not be asking the government to fix it, they'd only add forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it makes our farm harder to keep going. If the big potato growers run robots and sell cheaper, our prices drop further. We don't have the money for machines, and I wouldn't know how to run them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tighten our belts at home, no new phone for Daniel, and walk more instead of driving. I'd put in extra hours at the farm to save on the contractor at lifting time. Otherwise I'd wait and see, because I don't trust anything that's still being sold to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a cold coming on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd not ask the government. Who would you turn to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first, then the church. When the Hendersons' barn burned, the whole parish turned out and had it roofed in a month. That's worth more than any scheme from an office that's never seen a cow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Daniel's fourteen. What would you say to him about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn a trade, a proper one, with his hands. Plumbing, maybe, or electrics. And to come to the farm on Saturdays so it doesn't die with Walter.

S1.say: He'd say big companies are doing what they always do and small farms must dig in. He wouldn't ask the government to fix it, expecting only more forms.
S1.think: Privately he thinks steady change makes the family farm harder to keep going, as robot-run growers drive potato prices down. They can't afford machines and he couldn't run them.
S1.do: Tightens spending at home, with no new phone for his son and more walking instead of driving. Works extra hours to save on the contractor, and otherwise waits to see what happens.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a cold coming on.
S1.quote: That's worth more than any scheme from an office that's never seen a cow.
S1.fieldNote: His safety net is family and parish, illustrated by a barn rebuilt by neighbours. He wants his son in a hands-on trade and connected to the farm. Distrust of both big business and government runs side by side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's man playing God, and it'll end badly. I'd say that at church and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the farm's finished as a business within a couple of years. Nobody will pay for hand-graded potatoes when a robot farm sells them for half. But the land is still the land, and Walter won't sell it, so we'd eat off it even if we can't live off it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd plant a much bigger vegetable garden and get a few pigs and hens for the family. I'd go back to Rick, my old foreman, and ask for any building work, since some of that might take longer to go. We'd cut everything, and Ruth and I would talk to Walter about whether we could move up to the farmhouse to save the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be praying a lot more, I'll say that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you don't want handouts. What if there were a government income for everyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hate it. I'd probably take it, if the kids needed shoes, and I'd hate myself for it. A man who's paid for doing nothing loses something you can't buy back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does it matter that this comes in two years rather than ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years and Walter's still alive, so the farm's still in the family and we can hide up there, in a way. Ten years and he's gone, and who knows. It's an odd thing, but the fast one might keep us together better.

S2.say: He'd call fast AGI man playing God that will end badly. He'd say so at church and mean it.
S2.think: Privately he thinks the farm would be finished as a business within two years, as robot farms undercut hand-graded potatoes. But the family land would remain, so they could eat from it even without income.
S2.do: Expands the vegetable garden and keeps pigs and hens for the family. Asks his old building foreman for work, cuts all spending, and discusses moving into the farmhouse to escape the mortgage.
S2.feel: Alarmed, and praying a lot more.
S2.quote: A man who's paid for doing nothing loses something you can't buy back.
S2.fieldNote: The family land is a fallback that thin savings alone wouldn't give him, which keeps him short of panic. He'd take state income only reluctantly, with real shame. He makes a surprising point: the fast picture might keep the family together better while his father-in-law is alive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for decent people to get ready without the government holding their hand. Teach the young ones trades, keep the land in families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm not sure five years helps me much. I'm no good with computers and I'm not about to start. It does give Daniel time to start a trade, and that's what I'd care about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get Daniel into an apprenticeship the day he's old enough, sixteen, and I'd ask around the parish who's taking lads on. I'd keep working the farm and grow more of our own food each year. I'd vote for whoever promises to keep family farms out of the hands of the big companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not sleeping well, but not falling apart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not about to start with computers. Is there anything that would change your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Walter told me to, maybe. He won't. Ruth says I'm as stubborn as the old bull, and the old bull is still here, isn't he?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big firms that build these things for profit and don't care who gets hurt. And people who stopped going to church and stopped knowing their neighbours, so there's no one to catch them. Not the robots, a robot's just a tool.

S3.say: He'd say five years is enough for decent people to prepare without government hand-holding. Teach young people trades and keep land in families.
S3.think: Privately he doubts five years helps him, since he won't take up computers. It matters because it gives his son time to start a trade.
S3.do: Gets his son into an apprenticeship at sixteen through parish contacts and keeps working the farm, growing more of their own food each year. Votes for whoever promises to protect family farms from big companies.
S3.feel: Anxious and sleeping badly, but not falling apart.
S3.quote: Ruth says I'm as stubborn as the old bull, and the old bull is still here, isn't he?
S3.fieldNote: He jokes about his stubbornness but holds firm. He blames profit-driven firms and a loss of community rather than the technology itself. The value of extra time is measured almost entirely by his son's future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and people should stop moaning and get on with it. Plant, build, teach your kids, same as our grandparents did with every change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years worries me in a different way. Walter won't be with us by then, and the farm goes to Ruth and her brother. Her brother would sell to the highest bidder, and that's a robot farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Walter now, while he's well, to sort out the will so the land stays farmed by family. I'd keep working, keep the garden going, get Daniel and Grace into trades or whatever lasts. I'd wait to see what the machines really do before I'd spend a penny on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's family worry more than robot worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: That's a hard conversation to have with Walter.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. I'd do it with Ruth there, after Sunday lunch. Talking about wills over the roast is miserable, but losing the ridge to a company is worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Grace is ten. What would you want for her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something that keeps her near home. She loves the calves, she'd be a vet if she could. If machines do the rest, I'd want her doing the thing where you need a kind hand.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is a long time and people should stop moaning and get on with it. Plant, build and teach your children, as earlier generations did.
S4.think: Privately ten years worries him differently, because his father-in-law would likely be gone and the land would pass to his wife and her brother. He fears the brother would sell to a robot farm.
S4.do: Asks his father-in-law now to arrange the will so family keeps farming the land. Keeps working and gardening, guides both children towards lasting trades, and waits before spending anything on machines.
S4.feel: Uneasy, more about family than about robots.
S4.quote: Talking about wills over the roast is miserable, but losing the ridge to a company is worse.
S4.fieldNote: With more time, the threat shifts from technology to inheritance and his brother-in-law. He'd tackle a hard family conversation rather than change his own work. His children's futures are framed around staying close to home.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, even though I said it might keep us together. It's too fast for anybody to think. What would help is less red tape for small farms and some way to keep land in families instead of being bought by companies. Help with apprenticeships for the kids, not handouts for me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. Whatever the machines can do, they won't sit with Walter when his time comes, and that's still our job.

headlineQuote: Whatever the machines can do, they won't sit with Walter when his time comes, and that's still our job.
portrait: Erik Lopez is a 43-year-old former builder's labourer who has worked his father-in-law's small beef and potato farm for five years, still learning and paid what the farm can spare. He lives in the village with his wife Ruth, who works at the church office, and their two children, with a mortgage and under a month saved. Traditional and wary of both big companies and government, he relies on family and parish rather than state help and never uses AI. He is calm in the plateau, uneasy with steady change and alarmed by two-year AGI, when he'd fall back on the family land. With longer timelines, his worry shifts to inheritance and to getting his children into hands-on trades.
biggestWorry: AGI within two years, because it would come too fast for anybody to think and would end the farm as a business.
whatWouldHelp: Less red tape for small farms, ways to keep land in families rather than sold to companies, and apprenticeships for his children.
